speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of thinking in the country now, and I believe it is taking hold quite broadly, that economic conditions are beginning to show signs of upward trends in North America. The signs seem to be becoming more positive all the time. One of these indicators is the expected pace of home building this year or, rather, the pace and the nature of home building in 1971. Nobody can deny that both are strong and healthy this year. Therefore, I think we might begin to recognize that quite a few things are going right in Canada too. Our expectations are that there will be 220,000 housing starts in Canada in 1971-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-which is well over the previous record of 210,000 starts in 1969. Moreover, the emphasis of the government on homes for the low in income, where the chief needs really are, will be continued. So, Mr. Speaker, there will be an accelerated and buoyant housing program in Canada this year. This accelerated program will pump substantially more jobs and more spending into the Canadian economy and its effects will be felt quickly at a time when jobs are the Canadian priority. Jobs are the absolute Canadian priority right now, Mr. Speaker, and caring for and response to the most felt needs of today mark what we must do.
Equally important, when the people most in need of our concern are those who must worry most about decent shelter as well as jobs, a very large part of the building activity will be directed to modest and low-income housing. I am talking about home ownership for low to middle-income families, public housing and low rental housing. This is our thrust. Its benefits will reach importantly into Canadian society over the long haul and in trying to deal with today's most urgent needs. These prospects are reflected in the 1971 capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which I now wish to table in the House. This budget is the federal government's main
strategic instrument for affecting the housing conditions of Canada and for helping to shape urban form and process. Because we have followed a target of at least one million new homes over the five years 1970 to 1974, increasing federal assistance when the private market slackened as it did last year, we have kept house production and mortgage flow on a more even keel. We are beginning to find ways to avoid the old boom and bust cycles.
This year's total budget is $942 million, represented by $902 million plus a previously announced $40 million, against the original 1970 budget of $854 million. It will assist in the production of about 220,000 starts during the year. There will be an expected 165,000 starts by a private market that is resurging as mortgage rates drop and mortgage money becomes significantly easier, and frankly, to my encouragement, as the lending institutions appear to be accepting their obligation to the social needs of housing as well as to profit opportunities. The remaining 55,000 housing units will be financed by CMHC in co-operation with our partners in the provinces and other sponsors. In addition, of course, to the $942 million capital commitment, the CMHC expenditure budget in 1971 is $67 million, as will appear in the estimates to be tabled shortly.
I would like to explore for a minute the economic impact of the residential building in store for this year. New housing construction has one of the highest labour contents of any major economic activity. Each new dwelling unit provides at least two man year's of employment on site and in the production of building materials. This is direct employment, which is only part of the story. In 1970, in spite of the forecasts of doom and disaster there were 190,000 units started, the third best year in Canada's history, despite the economic conditions that slowed down private market activity. The federal government played a major part in keeping the pace active last year. In August, as hon. members may remember, we extended the original 1970 CMHC capital budget by $240 million, the great bulk of which went to low-income housing.
In 1971, as I have said, the prospect is for 220,000 starts. In addition, from last year there are 148,000 dwellings under construction and to be completed during this year. In direct employment alone these starts and completions will mean a minimum increase of 60,000 man year's of employment in housing construction in 1971. The beauty is that house building work is turned on quickly. We have made estimates which show that from the approval of a loan to start of construction, to the employment of people, can be as little as 40 days and certainly under 90 days. The job-providing impact will be even higher in the first half of the year than for the whole year because of the work on dwellings already started. Of course, there are many indirect employment benefits as well. To cite a relatively small but important one, the residential building increase this year implies additional employment of about 2,000 man-years simply because people, when they move into new homes, spend about $1,600 per home on new furniture, appliances, drapes and the like Then further up the scale, this year's housing

February 10, 1971

program is equivalent to building a city of close to a million people. That bespeaks new or expanded streets, sewers, schools, shopping centres and other facilities and adds another 6,000 or more new jobs.
The biggest economic impact, one generally dispersed throughout the economy, comes from the spending of income by workers who would otherwise be unemployed. That provides another 70,000 or 80,000 man-years of new jobs. In all, Mr. Speaker, the new jobs created directly and indirectly simply by the increase in residential building activity will total 140,000 to 150,000 man-years. That is a very substantial part of the unemployment picture. Therefore, housing construction in 1971, in spite of all the derisive and almost wishful comments from the opposition, will greatly aid Canada's employment picture.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We told you that two years ago.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The pace of construction has a vibrant look this year, for several reasons. The federal government will directly support lower priced housing substantially again this year, almost to the exclusion of support for higher cost housing so far as the CMHC budget is concerned. The low to medium priced homes are not only where the need is but, as builders are rapidly learning, where the market is. The higher priced market is in many places overbuilt and demand is soft. The government, to provide housing but also to spur employment is pressing its housing program now. More and cheaper money is becoming available for private mortgages. I am in continuing contact with major lenders and major pension trusts who are showing signs of responding. They have given me strong indications that they are prepared to put large amounts of money into modest income housing.

speechtext:
I have mentioned the additional $240 million last August, funds which went mainly to the building of most income housing. Also, at the beginning of last year I reserved $200 million of CMHC mortgage funds for a special program to seek innovative ways to build homes for owning and renting by families earning as little as $4,000 a year. The plan worked well. Commitments under this program were made for just under
15,000	units with some carryover still to come. That had to be something of a crash program for we were forced to gear it to starts made during 1970 since the private market was slipping. But it provided excellent experience and lessons in new forms of tenure and land use, new methods of financing, imaginative mixes of commercial with residential building so that the commercial would help pay for the residential.
The Budget-Mr. Andras
Favourable National Housing Act lending terms of 71 per cent and 8 per cent were provided for the building of low-rental housing projects public housing, student housing, sewage treatment and land assembly projects. I am happy to announce, Mr. Speaker, that these special interest rates from today are lowered further, both to 75 per cent.
Innovation-the essence of our approach last year in the $200 million program-the search for and the incentives for new ways to build good housing cheaper, will continue to be sponsored by the government this year. For 1971, $558 million has been reserved for the provision of housing for low-income Canadians through sections 35 and 16 of the National Housing Act. Of this, $253 million has been allocated for provincial housing programs. Another $295 million is allocated for section 16 lending under the National Housing Act. Under this section non-profit organizations, governments, entrepreneurs and sponsor groups can evolve special housing projects for elderly people, families of low income and other disadvantaged persons. The relatively low interest charges make relatively low rents possible.
These funds will produce 38,000 housing units designed specifically for the low-income market. Thus, in the three years 1969-71 commitments will have been made for
113,000	such dwelling units. The measure of that progress is that only 82,000 such units were committed in all of Canada's time up to 1969. This is not to say I am satisfied or complacent, but it is a positive indication of progress.
In addition to the specifically designed low-income units, Mr. Speaker, we have increasingly been devoting funds under section 40 of the National Housing Act to low-income application. The allocation of funds for section 40 this year is $172 million. It is directed at new building in resource towns and small urban centres and also at the rehabilitation and/or purchase of existing homes anywhere in Canada. In addition to those self-contained housing units, the new budget-$789 million all told-will finance 14 450-bed hostels for elderly persons and students.
While the 1971 budget continues to give primary emphasis to housing concerns, it also provides $153 million for urban infrastructure. That includes $87 million for sewage treatment projects, $43 million for land assembly and $20 million previously committed to urban renewal. I would be the last to claim that the housing activities of a nation-still less of one government-could be adequately summed up in a listing or programs. I do believe, however, that following the important activities of my predecessor and his 1968-69 task force on housing and urban affairs-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and during the almost two years that I have held responsibility at the federal level for housing, major steps have been taken. A new importance is attached, countrywide, to the housing needs of Canadians, and not just by numbers. The climate or relations among all levels of government in focusing on these needs has perceptibly improved. In dramatically shifting

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Andras
emphasis to the housing needs of low-income Canadians, priorities have been clearly defined. More Canadians will either have to swallow their rhetoric on poverty or get in with us and support our efforts to provide more housing for people on low income.
I also urge the provinces and the municipalities to do more of that which only they can do. Let them make use of the national building code, which no other level of government can force upon them, for instance. Let provincial governments review the recommendations of the 1968-69 task force on housing. Nearly all the recommendations that were purely federal in scope have been implemented. It is true that some requiring provincial, municipal or private sector response have not been acted upon. We must all act in concert as much as possible. We recognize more than ever before that housing and all the complex environment of urban living is interspliced. like the structure of an atom, with many other issues such as jobs, poverty, pollution, transportation, education-the whole range of contemporary matters.
We at the federal level are seeking every possible method of defining real need wherever it exists and trying to meet those needs, whether it is a study of the housing needs of Metis people in Alberta or Saskatchewan, the disadvantaged in the territories or the very special requirements, of the old people. The fact is that these needs should never be treated as simple, single and isolated one from the other. Therefore, no one level of government is capable of coping in isolation from the others. As our cities and city systems grow larger, and there is every indication that that is the way we are heading, that factor of interdependence will become ever more the case.
These complexities are what should be discussed and, who knows, resolved by a much closer working together of the various levels of government. We are starting such a process with the provinces. We hope that preliminary talks now going on will result in a trilevel-federal, provincial and municipal-meeting on urban problems and priorities later this year. These discussions, Mr. Speaker, can well influence National Housing Act programs as we move toward careful and deliberate efforts to order together our urban lives.
If I may sum up, we forecast 220,000 starts this year. We forecast an increase, as a result of this increase in starts, of between 140,000 and 150,000 man-years of work. That means more jobs, which are needed most of all in this country today. The budget will be $942 million. The capital budget of CMHC will continue to emphasize the need for us to work with the private sector in the provision of housing in the low-income sector where there is a great need. May I have the permission of the House to table the capital budget for 1971 of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in both official languages?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the minister, before tabling that document, would permit a question. Having listened
to the minister's impassioned appeal to the provinces and other bodies to get behind the housing program, may I ask him why the Manitoba government, which submitted proposals for a $55 million public housing project, has just been informed by CMHC that because of the unavailability of sufficient funds this project is being reduced to $31 million, which is a reduction of 40 per cent? In view of the minister's appeal to the provinces to get busy, it seems to me that this is not the best way to encourage them to support public housing and thereby increase employment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the optimist sees the doughnut and the pessimist sees the hole. I would have been delighted to have been able to give Manitoba the exact sums asked for, because they are embarked on a sophisticated five-year planning program, which we encourage. We are giving them three times as much as we gave them last year. Notwithstanding the $942 million budget, we had to make some allocations. Most provinces have asked for more than we can give them out of that budget. It was ever thus. I share the hon. member's concern that there are certain constraints within the budget. It is, nevertheless, very, very satisfactory.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I understand that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) is seeking permission to ask the minister a question. Is it agreed that the hon. member shall have permission to ask a question before the hon. minister resumes his seat?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have raised this question with the minister from time to time. It has to do with increased federal assistance for the rehabilitation of existing housing stocks. The minister mentioned this matter in his speech today. In view of the great importance of a vigorous rehabilitation of the housing program to help us meet the unemployment crisis, can the minister say whether vastly expanded action in this field is contemplated by the government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is our intention-and my reference to this matter was deliberate in the statement I made-to emphasize that the rehabilitation approach will be escalated over anything we have done in the past.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras). I only wish that I could share his optimism about the state of the Canadian economy. I have very serious doubts whether that optimism is shared by the hundreds of thousands of unemployed people who are walking the streets of Canada today. He suggested that the interest rate on housing loans will be lowered to 7J per cent. I think that is a very worthwhile objective. As a matter of fact, it should have been done many years ago. But what is the point of lowering the interest rate to

February 10, 1971

7j per cent when hundreds of thousands of people cannot afford to borrow the money and cannot afford to pay any interest, let alone interest at 7\ per cent?
Today, Mr. Speaker, we face a real crisis in Canada so far as unemployment is concerned. It is a crisis which in many respects is as serious as the one we faced in the so-called hungry thirties; a crisis which is growing worse every month and which is causing an awful lot of misery for thousands of Canadian families; a crisis the blame for which can be laid entirely at the feet of this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The blame can be laid at the feet of a government led by a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has said to the Canadian people, "If you don't like it, lump it."

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That, apparently, is the government's attitude to many people who find themselves unemployed. This is a government that is led by a man who just a few days ago is reported to have used disgusting and disgraceful language to a group of people who were only exercising their democratic right to parade on Parliament Hill and make known their grievances to the people and to the government. It is a government, Mr. Speaker, under the leadership of a Prime Minister who is obviously losing the confidence and respect of the Canadian people. If he were doing his duty, I suggest that he ought to resign and let the people of Canada determine whether they are satisfied that this government is doing all it can in the interests of our unemployed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our massive unemployment today, Mr. Speaker, was not created by the people of Canada, nor was it created by labour. It was created by this government, the government which created tight money, the government which pushed interest rates sky high, the government which over the years has increased taxes and is continuing to increase them, the government which has limited the supply of money and has placed a very severe restraint on federal spending. Yes, it has been caused by the government. One would expect that the Prime Minister and his government would accept responsibility for this. Apparently, however, they do not wish to do so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is listening.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said in this House not long ago that everything is on the up and up and that everything will soon iron itself out. I ask him to tell that to the almost 600,000 people who are today unemployed and walking the streets, not knowing what to do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are told to live on $30 a week.
The Budget-Mr. McQuaid

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I ask him to tell that to the men and women who are out of work and whose families are suffering. This is through no fault of their own but, rather, to the lack of attention by this government to the problems of unemployment. There may be no crisis for the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, but there is a crisis for hundreds of thousands of Canadians and their families. Figures bear out the fact that the year 1970 was one of general slowdown in the Canadian economy. This slowdown was brought about by the fiscal and monetary policies of this government. We were told that these policies were adopted to fight the so-called inflationary trend. The result is that we are now suffering a slow growth in our economy. We are also suffering a very high rate of unemployment.
According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, 155,000 more people were unemployed in December, 1970, than in December 1969. This represents an increase in unemployment of 40 per cent in one year. It is a disgraceful situation. Yet the government is not prepared to do anything substantial about it. In December, 1970, there were
62,000	more people unemployed than in the month of November. This represents an increase, in one month, of 14 per cent. But the government is apparently not prepared to do anything about it. The rate of unemployment in this country is more critical than in the worst years of the depression.
A very large proportion of the unemployed are the youngest people in the labour market. Almost 20 per cent of the registered unemployed are 19 years of age or younger. I suggest it is a very serious matter when 20 per cent of our young people are introduced into an atmosphere of forced idleness. Many of them do not want to be unemployed, but there isn't anything for them to do. At one time only the unskilled were unemployed. That is not the situation today. Many of our better educated people are unemployed. There are unemployed people walking the streets today with university degrees as high as doctorates. They are unable to find work. The unemployment situation in Canada is serious.
I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to the very serious situation in my area, Atlantic Canada. There has been a very serious increase in unemployment in that area. The number of unemployed increased from 42,000 in November to 54,000 in December, an increase of 12,000 in one month. That is the largest monthly increase of unemployment in the Atlantic provinces since 1956. The government has done very little about the increase in unemployment in the past 14 years. The rate increased from 6.3 per cent in November to 8.3 per cent in December. The rate in that area was the highest in Canada, with the possible exception of the province of Quebec. The latest figures available for my province of Prince Edward Island are for March 31, 1970. At that time there were 8,959 people receiving social assistance. Many of these almost 9,000 people were willing but unable to find work. In order to support themselves and their families they had to lower themselves to the point where they had to ask the government for social assistance. That is

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. McQuaid
the highest figure of any province with the exception of Newfoundland. In March, 1970, 16.2 per cent of the people of Newfoundland were receiving social assistance. In Prince Edward Island it was 8.1 per cent; Nova Scotia, 6.2 per cent; New Brunswick, 8.1 per cent. The average in the Atlantic area at that time was 9.6 per cent. Almost 10 per cent of the people received social assistance: they had no other means of supporting themselves or their families.
The situation with regard to social welfare in Canada is very serious. Statistics show that in the field of social welfare Canada is one of the highest per capita spenders in the world. The answer to our problem is not social welfare. I am convinced that if our spending in the social welfare field continues as it has in the past we will very soon be faced with a rude awakening. It is the responsibility of the government, indeed Parliament, to ensure that everyone who is willing to work has the opportunity to do so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The people of Canada only ask for the opportunity to earn a decent living for themselves and their families. To date this government has not done anything to provide that opportunity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not quarrel with the fact that welfare assistance is a necessity for the sick and the unemployable. However, it is time we devised a formula to provide employment for those who are capable of working and willing to work. There are hundreds of thousands of such people today in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a serious problem in Prince Edward Island. As hon. members know, we depend largely on agriculture to earn a living. There is a serious problem in so far as agriculture is concerned. I wish to quote some figures to make clear how serious this problem is. In 1930 the farm population in Prince Edward Island was 55,000. That figure represented 63 per cent of our population. By 1960, 30 years later, the farm population was reduced to 31,000, 28.1 per cent of our total population. Since 1960 it has continued to decline at a very alarming rate. In 1931 there were 12,865 occupied farms in our province. Today there are less than 5,000, a decrease of almost 8,000.
Unfortunately, the situation is not improving. As Your Honour knows, we depend very largely on our potato industry and that industry at this moment is being dealt a serious blow up, I would say, a small group of general store operators in Toronto who are apparently doing their best to promote the sale of Ontario potatoes. Let me give hon. members an example of how this is being brought about. Yesterday Prince Edward Island farmers were receiving 31 cents for a 10-pound bag of potatoes delivered in Toronto. These potatoes were selling on the Toronto market for 50 cents; that is to say, at a profit of
19 cents to the retailer. Ontario farmers were receiving 30 cents for a 10-pound bag of Ontario potatoes, only one cent less than the P.E.I. farmers were receiving, and Ontario potatoes were selling on the Toronto market for 39 cents. In other words, retailers were making 19 cents on P.E.I. potatoes, when they could sell them, though they were prepared to sell Ontario potatoes at a profit of only nine cents for a ten-pound bag.
This, of course, puts P.E.I. potatoes at a disadvantage despite their exceptional quality, because people will not pay 50 cents for a 10-pound bag of potatoes if they can buy reasonably good potatoes for 39 cents. As a result, our potato farmers estimate they will suffer a loss of some $5 million this year. I cannot help wondering whether the price of P.E.I. potatoes is not being deliberately pushed up in Ontario in order to promote the sale of Ontario potatoes. I do not know whether there is anything the government can do about it-I am not laying this at the feet of the government-but I do hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) will take notice of what is happening, and if the federal government can do anything to overcome this injustice I hope that action will be taken as soon as possible; otherwise, P.E.I. farmers will not be able to stay in business and the number of unemployed will be increased.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member mind answering a question? While I agree with many of the things he has said about the need to end regional disparity, does he consider he is being completely fair when he blames all unemployment problems on the present government? I have looked at the charts and find that the percentage of unemployed in the United States is even greater. And our federal government has nothing to do with what is happening in the United States; there is a Conservative administration there.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am blaming this government for not doing enough to overcome the unemployment problem as it exists in Canada. The necessary concrete measures are not being taken on behalf of people who are looking for work and who are able to work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a new member, his maiden speech in the House is perhaps an unforgettable occasion and I think that all members who went through this before me would agree that they have been deeply moved by this experience.
It is certainly gratifying for me to represent my constituency of Labelle in Parliament, but it also vests me with the responsibility for measuring up to my predecessor, the hon. Leo Cadieux, who fulfilled his duties in this House with remarkable zest. I wish to pay due tribute to him and to renew the testimony of admiration from his constituents of Labelle who have so often taken pride in the way he discharged his duties as Minister of National Defence and we are sure that he will brilliantly represent our country in Paris.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank all the members for the very warm reception they gave me in the House after my

February 10, 1971

election on November 16 last. I have been reassured by their liberal welcome and I wish that all members of the opposition who applauded on this occasion will not soon regret it.
May I also congratulate the hon. members for Fron-tenac and Lisgar (Messrs. Corriveau and Murta) who were brought to the House by the same by-election and may I wish them both a cloudless and fruitful career.
I will take advantage of a well-established tradition, on the occasion of a new member's first speech in the debate on the motion of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in directing my comments especially to my constituents in Labelle with the hope that all Canadians who believe in dialogue will also be listening. May I be allowed to express my gratitude for their so generous support, their loyalty to my leader and my party, loyalty they so eloquently expressed on November 16 and which can be found in my province and everywhere else in Canada.
Despite the successful result I obtained in this by-election on account of the great popularity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I do not forget the obligations and responsibilities I accepted.

Mr. Speaker, the riding I have the privilege of representing in this House, and which was so ably represented by my predecessor, is composed of 50 municipalities ranging in terms of population from the highly industrialized city of St. Jerome to a large number of renowned summer and winter resorts in the heart of the Laurentian mountains and small villages and settlements six miles south of Mont Laurier. It is, as closely as one can find, an accurate demographic reflection of the province of Quebec on a smaller scale.
Our population is composed of proud Quebeckers who are loyal and deeply-rooted Canadians. I can advance this assertion without hesitation, having known a vast number of them, having been brought up in the area and having lived in that part of the province for most of my life. We are the descendants of settlers who came to that region at the very beginning, settlers who plowed the land with courage, perseverance and an expectation which was not always rewarded in accordance with the full measure of their efforts.
Our history is, in a way, similar to that of the first Canadians who explored and developed this great land in which various ethnic groups are represented. In fact, most of the elements to be found in the Canadian mosaic, the largest proportion being French-speaking, all have, with their particular talent and ability, contributed in large measure to the development of our region. Together we have adjusted to the accelerated evolution of our time, although for all of us the first and utmost priority is still economics.
If Canada is rich on account of the diversity of its population, my constituency is largely endowed in this regard and shares such wealth with the rest of this country.
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
An important part of the constituency of Labelle, Mr. Speaker, enjoys a long-standing tourist tradition known throughout this country, on account of its great beauty, its numerous lakes full of various species of fish and the majestic Laurentian mountains.
We believe our constituency is the most visited in this country, by our fellow citizens of other provinces as well as by our neighbours to the South. The best known tourist establishments in the province are in our constituency, a few miles north of Montreal.
The construction of the new Montreal airport and the economic upsurge that should follow for the whole area compel us to think of what the future has in store for us. We must ensure that our existing facilities will be able to meet the soaring demand from our citizens who are anxious to enjoy the countryside and come closer to nature and who increasingly insist that all those natural beauties which are so many features of our region be preserved and made accessible to them.
As economic requirements force us to alter our environment, those elements become more important to our mental health, to our return to wilderness and to an environment not spoiled by man.
Mr. Speaker, it seems that this ambition is being voiced by influential people in this region who want a major part of the territory to be turned into a genuine national park similar to those existing throughout the country. This undertaking will have a dual impact: the creation of permanent jobs for skilled people already dedicated to tourism and proud of its tradition and consequent high repute and, for the most densily populated area of North America, the provision of a holiday resort second to none. This ambitious project is winning more and more supporters in all quarters, and it is becoming more and more difficult to resist the trend.
In our area, close to holiday resorts, there is a huge territory well suited to that kind of development, involving no danger of ecological unbalance and remarkable for its climate, topography and wildlife.
The tourist industry, one of the main industries in the province, in which we have specialised and acquired a reputation, seems now to offer more security than many others which, on account of changing times, are no longer important sources of employment. We must pave the way in that field and protect this source of foreign currency. We should be prepared to meet the needs of the people in our area who want well-paid work and job security.
During the last few years, we have faced rather serious employment difficulties caused mainly by an important migration of farm hands and labourers from the North of the riding who believed that they could find greater employment opportunities in Saint-Jerome. That exodus has had the effect of greatly increasing the unemployment rate.
As all other Canadians, Mr. Speaker, we are concerned with the yearly increase in seasonal unemployment. That situation is ascribable to many factors which hon. members of the opposition have not identified. Reports indicate especially that agriculture in Canada has been losing
24,000	jobs a year since 1955. That is mainly due to a

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
greater availability of capital, to automation and to a greater efficiency.
Unemployment is caused both by fluctuations in demand, as severe here as in the countries where we export, as well as by the work reduction factor in production, technological changes, labour mobility, depletion of natural resources in a given area, changes in management and ownership of undertakings which leads to the disappearance of some manufacturers.
We must also ask ourselves whether the unions, with their requests for ever increasing wages for fewer and fewer employees, do not contribute to a large extent to reducing the labour force. I suspect that disproportionate union demands force the employers to excessive efficiency, which leads to smaller staffs, which are better paid, I agree, but which are more exposed to unemployment. Would it not be better if the unions would rather have more men paid decent wages than fewer workers drawing higher pay?
To that one can add the continuous increase in the number of multiple jobs. That is too often the case with people holding two or more jobs, the wife and husband sharing the financial burden of the family with the income each of them has. In Canada we once had the highest employment increase among industrialized countries, but in spite of this increase, in 1970, as everyone knows, the unemployment rate reached 5.9 per cent compared to 4.7 in 1969. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, in 1961 the national unemployment rate was 7.2 per cent, and 9.3 in my province. Of course, unemployment must be the concern of everyone, because of its implications on the social structure. Also, the people of my province who exert themselves in opposing any measure conducive to the right atmosphere for creating the famous 100,000 jobs, should be despised by the unemployed. We must ask if those people see, beyond statistical data, the human anguish, the solitude, the alienation and even often the desperation of the human beings those figures represent. We hope they understand that people on welfare are permanently branded with indignity.
I am thinking about those who, for obscure reasons, oppose the construction of the East-West expressway in Montreal, those who by their loud statements perpetuate this atmosphere of uncertainty to which is due the crisis of October last, brought about over the last few years by the verbal violence of petty politicians who remind us of the so-called "conquerors of the useless". There is also this too common attitude whereby employment is a right rather than an elementary duty which fulfils and glorifies human beings.
tEnglish]
Of course, those, fanatical people with dreamer's eyes who desire change for the amusement they find in pulling things to bits make pandemonium and call it progress. Society is satiated with quacks and their quick cure-alls, the like of them being responsible for many ills in Europe of yesteryear. These conflicts, insecurities and frustrations which are the difficult legacy of the Canadian youth have at least one positive aspect: they are in a
sense the growing pains of evolving cultures. These very difficulties provide the impetus for a constructive search for new cultural forms. Today, social institutions are extremely complex and no single approach provides a complete understanding of them. Countless young people find themselves confused. They see an apparent disintegration of hitherto solidly established codes and traditions. They sense that their elders are bewildered and perplexed.
No one has ever been young before in such a world. Both young and old wonder what brought about the present state of things, and the young have an itch for activity that will make the future brighter. The great majority of young people show an awareness of what is going on and a mature understanding.
The crisis in human affairs that confronts every generation anew is never as new as it seems to that generation. There were equally spectacular political, economic and social changes and equally showy transformations of dress and manners in other ages, some long past. People talk about new generations as though they were separate waves, but they are not: they flow into each other and each new generation has many good qualities and thoughts to exchange as it overlaps and merges with the previous one. Every period of life has its problems and its solutions, and the benefits which flow from these solutions are available only to those who are pliable. Someone once said that old or young, we have to keep flexible in living our lives, not flexible as to principles or as to things of eternal truth but flexible in our reactions to environment, to people and places, to the going and coming of friends and family and to changing situations and circumstances.

The Canadian dream, Mr. Speaker, is the establishment of a democratic society within which men know how to govern themselves and are free to achieve self-improvement to the full extent that their capabilities and energy will permit, with the objective to promote well-being in the population, according to similar principles of decency, freedom and equality.
When looking at our gigantic country and its numerous development possibilities, we sometimes get the impression that we are midgets playing on a stage designed for titans. This could perhaps explain the attitude of some of my fellow-citizens who have thrown in the towel because they do not believe they can meet the challenge.
Our Canadian mosaic is not an obstacle, but a positive factor in the task of building a great nation.
Civilized people accept, Mr. Speaker, that their neighbors have opinions which differ from theirs. They are free from this mental disease, the symptoms of which are total intolerance toward the views of other people.
Not only is it important to believe passionately in democracy, but also to practise it earnestly. In this society of ours, the individual may, by participating in government and by being educated, realize more than ever his role as a citizen.

February 10, 1971

People cannot live happily in isolation. That is why Jewish prayers insist on plural rather than singular forms, on community rather than on individuality.
Where questions of substance are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we may say that most Canadians pay respect to the same values. They believe in a social order in which individuals are more important than objects, in which ideas are more important than slogans, in which individuals are judged on their personal values and in which men may express their opinions under the protection of the law.
The Canadian way of life offers one method of having intelligence, good will and individual efforts work towards solutions to the problems. Success depends on whether we may expect that the ordinary citizen will act to the best of his knowledge, that he will do his duty and that he will perform it intelligently.
Then, as people say on our coasts, the rising tide will get all boats afloat.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to commend the hon. member for his first speech in the House.
In his remarks, he mentioned, among those who create verbal difficulties for a job-creating economic organization, those who objected to the proposed East-West expressway in Montreal. If I have interpreted his remarks faithfully, can the hon. member tell us whether his criticisms were aimed at the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), the Liberal member for Hochelaga, who was the first, as cabinet minister, to object to this proposal?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my remarks were not aimed at anybody in particular. I do not recall referring to anyone or naming anyone. I meant all those who object to this proposal being implemented as soon as possible. [EngZish]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the new member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) on his maiden speech. It was an excellent speech and I am certain that much thought went into it. It was idealistic and intelligent. I am certain that members of the House who heard him share my sentiments. His comments were positive and optimistic.
Unfortunately, I have to turn now to a matter which I cannot greet with optimism and confidence. I find myself somewhat limited in expressing my sincere anger and unhappiness at the current state of our unemployment picture. I cannot express myself well because all the best adjectives have already been used by previous speakers. We have heard words like "criminal", "immoral", "tragic", "insensitive", "technocratic", "vicious" and "callous". All these have been hurled at the government, and I think rightly so. These word weapons are the only weapons at the disposal of the opposition to get the government to respond to the crisis of unemployment facing 700,000 Canadians.
The Budget-Mr. Rose
I know that these words fall on deaf ears. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) told us that he has heard them all before. The wives, children and families of 700,000 Canadians are facing a desperate crisis this winter, and 23 per cent of all those unemployed Canadians happen to live in my province of British Columbia. The other day when the Minister of Finance was speaking about his budget he accused the opposition of attempting to make political capital out of the tragedy of this issue. What does he expect Members of Parliament in the opposition to do-sit silently by and accept it all? If one thinks of it in more concrete terms than the abstract figure of 700,000 people, you realize that this is roughly the population of Vancouver, which is Canada's third largest city. Here we have a metropolis of people who are bitter, idle, deprived and degraded, not by chance, not by acts of God-unless you consider the cabinet a many-headed god-but by the deliberate, premeditated, inhuman economic policies of this government. You do not have to use the words of the opposition to document this. The classic remark made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) at the time we debated this matter previously testifies to this fact. The minister said, "It takes courage for a government to create unemployment." What a line that is!
We speak today rather belatedly on this issue, not because we did not know it all before, not that we did not know it was coming but because last fall suddenly we had problems in Canada and people were in no frame of mind to listen seriously to this issue. We were preoccupied with the problem in Quebec. People might have listened to unemployment predictions if they themselves had been unemployed, but the average Canadian was not yet touched by it. He was touched, however, by the FLQ crisis. I happen to believe that the FLQ crisis, the so-called apprehended insurrection, was blown up out of all proportion by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for reasons best known to himself, his buddies, his confidants. Our Prime Minister is experienced in show biz. Just as he did last fall in the Quebec crisis situation, I would now like him to use his talents to give a lead in arousing all Canadians to the far more pernicious and widespread personal crisis of no work and push this to its true perspective, because in my view in the long run joblessness is far more serious. There is no point in the Minister of Finance or any other minister trying to cover it up or to explain it away with some sort of sophisticated sophistry. As hon. members on all sides of the House know, unemployment is very real and widespread. It reaches into every hamlet, village and city throughout the land, with tremendous waste and leaving a legacy of despair that will last for years to come. You do not get over being out of work in a hurry.
I do not believe there is a family in Canada that has not a relative or friend untouched by the grim hand of unemployment. There is the husband who has received his notice from Air Canada and then fails to get unemployment insurance. There is the son who dedicated himself to get an education or a trade and who now finds there is no job for his particular skill. Some people's sons

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Rose
have even had to move in with their parents. They are the lucky ones. Some parents do not have room for them in their houses. What about the merchant who has to lay off a long term employee or who has to close his business because customers do not appear at his door in sufficient number? What about the farmer, unskilled, chased off the land, adrift in an urban environment because of the enclosure policies with respect to agriculture devised by the government? The same applies to the fishing industry.
Ask the guy lining up at the unemployment insurance wicket for welfare, or at the soup kitchen, who is to blame. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) found out when he visited Vancouver, the answer is that the worker's misfortune is due to politicians. An unemployed man no longer believes his problems are his own fault, nor does he distinguish between members of the government and members of the opposition-again something that the Leader of the Opposition found out. He lumps us all together. He no longer believes in the conventional mythology of the Protestant ethic that being unemployed is his own fault, not the government's, and is due to some failure in his own personality. He brands all politicians as a bunch of useless, parasitic individuals. And if opposition members follow the advice of the Minister of Finance and fail to speak out, knowing our words are going to fall on deaf ears because of the government's obstinacy, then we will be parasites. It is our job to talk about this matter and no amount of advice from the Minister of Finance will prevent us from doing it.
The government has taken all the credit for retarding inflation. It seems to me only just that if it wants to bask in the euphoria of having accomplished its deflation goal, it must also accept the major responsibility for causing much of the current unemployment. I do not see how the government can have it both ways. This "no work" crisis was brought about as a direct result of the government's exclusive preoccupation for the last 2J years with balanced budgets and inflation-fighting.
As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance entertained us the other afternoon. He blamed the problem of unemployment on Canada's severe winters. He blamed it on labour disputes. He forgot about the labour disputes in previous years, and the winters too. It may be convenient for him to do that. He blamed it on almost anything except on what in fact has been its major cause, the deliberate economic slowdown and austerity measures which have been high priority items of the government. The government cannot escape this and we are not going to let it escape it. The government did it. It did it deliberately. It knew full well the risk, in its policies of unemployment, of human redundancy.
A while back the Prime Minister was so committed to the government's economic policy that he was prepared to see unemployment go to 6 per cent. Well, he succeeded beyond his wildest dreams. In December, unemployment across Canada was 6.6 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis and predictions were that things would become worse and not better. We expect the announcement tomorrow of another seasonally adjusted figure. Perhaps
that figure will be lower, but the total number of unemployed will go up. Just ask the guy who is out of work how it feels to be seasonally adjusted! We can hardly blame him for being seasonally maladjusted. He becomes unhappy every winter.
The Minister of Finance claims that Canada has been outstanding in the western world in providing more jobs per capita. I cannot quarrel with his figures-but tell that to the guy in the soup-kitchen. Tell that to the municipalities I represent, where welfare costs have tripled over the past three years. The other day I received in the mail the welfare officer's report to the Langley municipal council, an area which I represent. I quote:
The chairman presented this report which showed the percentage of population in receipt of welfare for the month of December, 1970, was 9.95 per cent. This compares with 9.34 per cent in November and 7.64 per cent in December, 1969.
The figure now has increased by roughly 2 per cent. This is not dealing with costs: it deals with the number of people applying for welfare. I am sure this sad story is repeated through all the nine municipalities I represent. Some yeras ago the winter works program was withdrawn. We were told it would not be missed because millions of dollars would be devoted to manpower training and retraining. Now a lot of municipalities would like winter works programs reinstated because they are starved for funds for capital projects. My province is fortunate; it is to get 23 per cent of the $150 million loan fund recently announced. In fact, as was said today, we may get even more if other provinces do not fully use their share. But, Mr. Speaker, we must be fair about this matter. I am always fair, impartial and non-political when dealing with matters such as this and I point out that the tripling welfare costs in B.C. cannot be laid entirely at the door of the federal government.
By a stroke of a pen, three years ago the B.C. government, by changing a formula, doubled the cost of welfare to municipalities. Until then they were required to pick up 10 per cent of the welfare costs; but that was increased to 20 per cent. Now in Mr. Bennett's most recent budget that has been cut by 5 per cent. Municipalities will have to pick up only 15 per cent of the cost. I imagine he will receive great applause all around for that-but it is like the old story of the man who kept hitting himself on the head because it felt so good when he stopped. I think the policies of the federal government can be blamed for at least half of this increase which the municipalities must meet. As I have said, capital projects have been delayed in the municipalities. People are beginning to make dark mutterings about work-for-welfare proposals because they are sick and tired of bearing excessive costs which they cannot meet, and they see little relief for the future. All the people of Canada in one way or other pay for the waste of manpower. But what about the things we need? We need pollution abatement, roads, housing, sewers-so it is not that there is no need for full employment. It is simply that there is no government will to produce full employment, and even if there were such a will there are no programs to put it into action.

February 10, 1971

Mr. Speaker, apart from the Prime Minister there are three men who should be responsible for doing something about the unemployment crisis. They are the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and, of course, the Minister of Labour. Why don't they have the courage to admit that they have bungled the job? Why do they gloss over it and say that things are going to look great in the future? If they had the courage to admit their mistakes and start afresh, everybody would respect them. They are only human. I truly believe that the Minister of Finance is human. Sometimes I wonder, but really I am convinced he is. Sometimes we on this side of the House make mistakes and I am sure we would allow the Minister of Finance the same human characteristics. I am certain that if Canadians were asked to make sacrifices for something positive, they would be prepared to do so. But they are not prepared to accept the continuous sophistry of the flim-flam men. If these three ministers will not admit that they have bungled or that they disagree with the policies put forward by the Prime Minister or the government, policies that have caused so much grief and hardship, and if they continue to stumble around under orders, doing things against their better judgment, they are little more than the reincarnation of the Three Stooges and should be regarded as such.
Mr. Speaker, other members have pointed out that in December there were 218,000 young people out of work. Most of them were looking for work. There is a relatively recent phenomenon, however, of the voluntarily unemployed youth. I do not know whether this stems from discouragement, but there are the check-outs, the dropouts, the goof-offs-those young people who are so cynical or discouraged about our system that they spend their time examining their navals, freeing their minds or using any other excuse for indolence. They are a serious problem. I think we should be talking about this phenomenon but I do not think this is the time to do it. However, we will have to face the reasons behind their alienation in the near future. The goof-offs are a relatively new phenomenon and I think they are in the minority.
What kind of things might we do for these young unemployed, Mr. Speaker? The first thing we should look at is the opportunity for them to make social and economic contributions in Canada's northland if programs were designed to employ them there. Anyone interested in what is happening in other countries might be interested in reading Farley Mowat's new book about Siberia. Changes must be made in the manpower retraining regulations to allow these young unemployed access to the retraining programs even if they have not been part of the work force for the required three years. That is a relatively simple amendment which would solve a lot of problems. I know there are some flaws in this proposal because we are accustomed to thinking that only those who lack skills are unemployed. This is not true. A previous speaker mentioned the plight of some professional and trades people. If it is suggested that the unemployed are skilled people, the reaction will be: What is the point of training more plumbers and electricians just
The Budget-Mr. Rose
to be unemployed at a time when we already have unemployed plumbers and electricians?
Some long-range planning is essential on the question of the overdevelopment of skills. Canada is somewhat like some of the emerging nations who while desperately needing the skills of their own people force those who have been trained to emigrate and seek a market for their skills elsewhere because their country is not sufficiently developed to employ them gainfully. Canada's difficulties in this area stem from the fact that we have had an historic dependence on imported skills and have thus neglected training people here. In effect, we stole our doctors, teachers and other skilled people from other countries. We should have been training these people ourselves. And now that we are, there is currently limited opportunity for them to be gainfully employed. Hopefully, this is a temporary situation but I would not bet on it.
Besides greater manpower access, Mr. Speaker, maybe we should face the fact that for a long time to come we will have a large number of young people unable to find employment. The Minister of Labour admitted that there would be some instability in our labour-intensive industries while they automated and retooled in order to compete with low-cost imports. He mentioned textiles in particular. If the industry cannot meet the competition now and has to automate, it will not use the number of workers it once did. Muscle power is no longer saleable, and maybe for a long time to come we will have to face the bleak prospect of underemployed youth. What are we going to do about it? First of all, we might face the prospect squarely and begin to shorten the labour lifetime of the average man. There are many more pleasant things to do, Mr. Speaker, than to spend 45 years locked to the treadmill of an unrewarding job. Why is it necessary for men to spend 45 years performing work in order to eat, raise their families and then die? Surely there is more to life than this. But for many people there is not.
I was intrigued by the recent United Auto Workers contract proposal of "30 and out". This suggestion would help young and middle-aged people alike and certainly it would be popular. The suggestion was this: Can't we arrange our affairs so that a man can complete his labour from age 20 to 50 or 25 to 55 and then be retired at three-quarters of his salary? More men would be willing to retire earlier if it did not mean facing severe financial hardship. There are a lot of pleasant things to do before a man dies after the age of 55 when he has raised his children and discharged his responsibility. I talked this idea over recently-it is not a radical one because the armed forces and the RCMP have done this sort of thing for years-with a friend of mine who is a railroader. His wife works because he cannot provide for their five children on his salary alone. He said that most of the guys who go to work with him are going through the motions waiting for retirement. They are fulfilling their obligations and they would jump at the chance of early retirement. I asked: Is the price of packing it in worth a criminal reduction in income? My friend went on to say that he would buy a camper and travel, thus helping tourism and, incidentally, allowing himself and his wife

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Rose
the opportunity of enjoying life a little before they are too old.
I do not see why we have not considered something like this much more seriously. If we can arrange things so that we can retire a Member of Parliament after six years with $3,690 a year, surely to God we can do the same thing for the average guy after 30 years on the job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think that would be logical. A security constable aged 55 in the House of Commons said to me that he would retire tomorrow if he could obtain three-quarters of his salary. I ask, why cannot we do this sort of thing? It would bring opportunities and benefits to our young people. We do not do anything for them now, Mr. Speaker. If we could give them increased opportunities they could be employed and build their future with confidence. It is no joke for them to be forced into retirement at the age of 55. What is the good of that?
I am no economist, Mr. Speaker, nor do I pretend to be one. No economist is required to tell the government of the despair and desperation encountered by many people today. The government may not like our talking about the staggering proportion of our idle work force, but the age of obedience disappeared with the coming of the age of aquarius and people will not remain silent and accept certain conditions any more. Confrontation is never far from their minds. Do not expect the unemployed to remain deferential if conditions do not improve markedly, and soon. If we do not act soon, Mr. Speaker, it would come as no surprise to me if violence were to erupt across the land. Some of that violence, I am afraid, may make the FLQ crisis look like a Sunday school picnic.
In addition to the suggestions I have brought forward, may I reiterate some of my leader's suggestions brought forward the other day. We do not want to make political capital out of the tragedy of unemployment. Hopefully, however, the government will listen to some of our suggestions. We think that the 3 per cent surcharge on income tax ought to be dropped. This surcharge is being perpetuated and very soon our people will think of it as a permanent tax: it will just be there. Also, what about inviting the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras) to use his influence for the dropping of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials? I know how costly that would be in terms of the projections that the Minister of Finance has made, but if this could be done at least for senior citizens' housing it would be greatly appreciated. If you dropped the tax you could build them 11 per cent larger accommodations for the same money. The minister in charge of housing today said that it is planned to build 38,000 public housing units. Our party supports that concept. Our people need public housing units. Yet that need shows something else: it shows that our economy is in such desperate straits that many people are being forced into low-cost public housing units because they have no hope of buying houses of their own.
