speechtext:
I thank hon. members, Mr. Speaker. I will do my best to conclude my remarks as quickly as possible. I had been making some suggestions and I had mentioned housing. That some of these public housing units have been most helpful is beyond question. Nevertheless, under existing loan arrangements the loan is repayable over 50 years, and as a result of interest rates the cost of these projects is tripled. These high costs also impose a severe strain on the budget of the societies concerned, the result being that those societies collect from their tenants far greater rents than would be absolutely necessary if the interest rates were lowered. The rents now are often greater than most tenants are able to pay comfortably. If we got rid of interest rates with respect to public housing units and senior citizens' housing units, we could lower rents. At present it is only the favoured few who are accommodated in senior citizens' housing. Many of the older people in our cities live in slums or under appalling conditions. As I say, only a favoured few are accommodated in senior citizens' housing. Also, why cannot we consider increasing amounts paid by way of unemployment insurance and do that now? There is talk that we are to do it in April, but why could we not do it now?
In these times when more than 3 per cent of our people are unemployed and when such unemployment seems to be part and parcel of government policy, why can we not assist municipalities by paying them 65 per cent of their welfare costs instead of the traditional 50 per cent? After all, the municipalities did not invoke this policy, the federal government did. The federal government has responsibility but it is the municipalities that must grapple with this problem. That is all that I have to say at this moment, Mr. Speaker. I do not know whether my remarks will make any difference. Hopefully, somebody is listening. Perhaps this is a dialogue of the deaf, but we must speak on these matters. If we appear to be making political capital out of them, perhaps that is the name of the game.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3 last, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) stated in the House with vigour and optimism his economic forecasts for Canada.
That was over two months ago already and nobody has caught a glimpse yet of the improvement that the minister said was coming. The economy remains stagnant, it staggers more and more and the most eloquent proof of it is the insoluble unemployment problem. Everybody talks about it, but nothing changes. This government seems to have been most successful in increasing the unemployment rate as a result of its epic struggle against inflation.
[Mr. Rose.i
February 10, 1971

He has now more difficulties in suppressing what he has himself brought on.
Mr. Speaker, these are unavoidable consequences of a government which fight theoretical enemies first instead of considering in a very concrete manner the true well-fare of the human being. It is not in the mathematical feats of the Minister of Finance that solutions are to be found but in reverting entirely to the true monetary concepts, those that give money its actual role which is to serve citizens by promoting production and distribution of goods.
All along his budget speech, the minister did not fail to emphasize how the budgeted expenditures would act as incentives for the economy.
The amount of $54 million allocated to the Unemployment Insurance Fund, he said, and I quote:
.. .will, as well, give an immediate and direct stimulus to the economy, the benefits of which will spread quickly right across the country.
He added that "the $150 million granted to the provinces will have the same result."
He therefore agrees with the principle of fighting the stagnation of the economy and even stimulating it by resorting to an increase in the purchasing power. That is the very advice we have given the government all along. Naturally, the economy needs that valuable and essential motor which is the purchasing power. Each citizen, having more money, spends more. All want to improve their lot; a greater need for products makes itself felt. Therefore industries wake up, organize themselves to fill the demand, hence the increase in jobs. That is simple, and we do not understand why the government does not implement the solutions which we advocate.
Against all logics, and even against sheer common sense, the natural and instinctive theories of Social Credit are rejected without considering and implementing them. A continued floundering in the obscure labyrinth of the present financial system is deemed preferable.
1 wish to quote a passage from the minister's speech, which illustrates this mathematical struggle:
A responsible government which is operating on a realistic basis has to be concerned about the total size of its net borrowing requirements. We have to guard against creating too rapid an expansion of the money supply, that is to say we have to guard against another encounter with the second obstacle to a rise in living standards ... a renewed surge of prices. The borrowing needs of the government must be covered by a combination of sales of securities to the banking system and to the public.
In a few years, when at long last monetary reform has been achieved, such words will appear naive. One will wonder how supposedly sensible people could tolerate such absurdities. They will say that the old campaigner was above all an expert in bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, the efforts made by the government in order to eliminate that famous problem of unemployment, the subsidies granted through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in order to put new life
The Budget-Mr. Matte
into industry, all this of course deserves our support especially when housing projects are being encouraged. We quite agree and we wish that this policy will actually enable more Canadians to enjoy the advantages inherent in home ownership.
We are therefore quite glad about the achievements in this field but there are still a few small gaps which I would like to point out to the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras). Earlier today, he entertained us about some splendid housing projects; however, these projects are somewhat minimized by the fact that they are not generalized enough.
No doubt a community as important as Montreal may have more pressing needs than others for housing but, to build them, the city must be able to borrow at lower interest rates.
Of course, we understand that. We also understand that a locality such as Quebec City must also have these possibilities. But I do not agree anymore when the same advantages are denied to regions whose needs are as high if not higher than those I just mentioned.
For instance, God only knows how the region of Trois-Rivieres-Shawinigan-Grand'Mere, in brief the whole Saint-Maurice Valley, needs, as do Montreal and Quebec City, a true economic incentive such as housing. It is, therefore, necessary that this gap be bridged immediately and not in the near future and that the home building industry in the Saint-Maurice Valley be offered lower interest rates comparable to those elsewhere in the country.
Mr. Speaker, I know that grants have been made at a lower rate of interest for building apartment houses. Of course it is for houses to let, with apartments to let.
But Mr. Speaker, if some individuals are willing to invest tremendous amounts of money to promote one-family housing, this is as important-if not more-as promoting construction of low rent apartments. For this is a material ideal well understandable on the part of young families and even of all families, I think. Such an ideal, namely to have a house of their own, to feel really at home, is normal but it will materialize only if the terms are such that people may buy those houses.
Now when people are ready to invest so as to provide houses of that kind for workers with an income ranging from $4,000 to $5,000, I believe that requires all the attention of the minister responsible for housing, and he should give unreserved support to builders and would-be investors, in order to help the worker with an average or less than average salary, so that he may also have a house of his own.
This is the gap I wanted to outline in this housing program, but again I wish to repeat that I support the government measure.
I also support the drive shown by the minister responsible for housing and I hope he will throw himself with even more vigour and dynamism in implementing his policy to increase construction in this country.

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Matte
The unemployment problem is being set forth in every detail by the whole community. The issue is so serious that, not long ago, the Quebec Minister of Labour even suggested that it could bring about revolution in some parts of the country before long.
Unfortunately, this may well be true and this is why we should absolutely pool our resources to come up with a real solution to this problem. It is a well-known fact that solutions are limited within our present fiscal and economic system. There are not many solutions. But if We seriously consider the possibility of bringing about jasic change in our fiscal and monetary principles, we shall reach a final, not a temporary solution.
For instance, when technological progress and automation are forcing a great number of workers out of their job, should we conclude that it is necessary and essential to steer clear of progress and give priority to manpower over automation? If we keep within our present economic concepts, we finally come to this nonsensical situation where the extent of technological progress and automation is linked to the necessity of maintaining a given number of workers in a given industry. What happens next? Inflation, unavoidably. Then production costs go up accordingly. This is why we should now consider progress in a completely different perspective.
With enough ingeniosity, and thanks to his God-given intellectual capacities, man will find out a way to produce more with less manpower; we should be grateful to Providence and the genius of man. But since machinery is replacing the arms of man, why should the profits earned by machinery not be distributed to men?
Mr. Speaker, this principle that, in their usual language, Creditistes call a distribution of the purchasing power, of dividends, would if it were followed give us the possibility of eliminating unemployment, because we are in a dead-end street.
Must we spurn modern technology in order to have full employment, or change the system? If we are smart enough to replace ten men by a machine operated by only one worker, let us distribute the financial benefits brought about by this conversion to those ten workers. There is a normal way to consider life. And until these fundamental principles are applied, Mr. Speaker, I fear that a genuine solution will never be found. All the more since the present unemployment rate, which is given by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, is far from representing the actual unemployment rate, if one considers that the samplings which are made in order to identify this unemployment rate may not be adequate, if one considers that a good many unemployed do not bother to register anywhere, either because they know that they cannot qualify for unemployment benefits, so they do not register, or because they know that it is useless to inquire for a job at the Manpower Centre.
But where are we going to find and count these unemployed? The rate that is given is in my opinion well under the actual rate, especially as it is recognized that there are now from 500,000 to 600,000 unemployed people in Canada. Taking into account the fact that a good many are not accounted for in the statistics, I would say then
that there must be at present, in Canada between 800 and
900,000	unemployed and since each unemployed person has the responsibility of at least another person, it may be said that more than 2,000,000 people are directly affected by this plague called unemployment.
And when one has been living for the last couple of years through this idiotic fight unleashed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and based on an increase in unemployment as a means to combat the inflationary balloon, one knows what it is all about. And today, a cure is being sought for this disease which has now become just about incurable.
Nevertheless, we are still optimistic and we are prepared to offer our full and complete co-operation to the government so that by its action it may effectively fight unemployment and in this way help workers and all those in need to live a better life, even more so when we consider that in a land of plenty such as ours, it is absolutely shameful and still even more disheartening to have to starve in the midst of unparalleled plenty.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in the budget debate is prompted by the failure of this Parliament to provide sufficient financial resources to deal with one of the most dangerous threats to our environment. I refer to solid waste and the problem of its disposal. The growing piles of garbage in this country have a potential for harm even greater than the pollution of our air and water. It is true that during the life of this Parliament we have dealt at some length with the question of the pollution of our air and water, but we have not yet come to grips with the problem I am discussing today. Perhaps the present order of priorities was inevitable since the attention focussed on the belching smoke from municipal dumps and incinerators, and water quality research into the effects of land fill, first prompted some of the concern felt today with regard to the disposal of solid waste.
The matter to which I am directing attention has been brought before the House twice within the last year by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) by way of private member's motion and I would like to commend that member for his foresight and perseverance. The motion proposed by the hon. member called upon the government to initiate a national research and development program in respect of methods of proper and economic solid waste disposal, including studies directed to the conservation of natural resources by reducing the amount of waste and unsalvageable materials and recovering and utilizing potential resources in solid waste and-I think this is especially important

to provide technical and financial assistance to provincial and municipal governments and multigovernmental agencies in the planning, development and conduct of solid waste disposal programs. I believe that such a program should be funded by the federal government through the soon-to-be-created department of the environment.
(Mr. Matte.]
February 10, 1971

It has been argued that this is basically an urban problem. Strictly speaking, this is not true because a formal definition of the term "solid waste" would include mineral and agricultural waste. These two categories account for roughly 90 per cent of the solid waste produced in this country and this waste is usually found in the rural and less developed areas. The other 10 per cent which is made up of residential, commercial, institutional and industrial waste represents perhaps the most serious problem in that it is concentrated in our few heavily populated urban areas. Everywhere people live and work, solid waste builds up and most Canadians live and work in a few urban centres. Surveys show that 1,000 pounds of solid waste are produced annually for every man, woman and child in Canada. This figure is climbing each year, largely because of an improving standard of living.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about cabinet waste?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Combine this fact with the prediction that by the year 2000 about 90 per cent of Canadians will live in urban areas and it is easy to see that we have quite a problem on our hands-a problem that will not go away just because we do not have the intergovernmental apparatus to deal with it. We have solved these problems before and we can do it again. In fact, we must do it again. The costs to city and regional governments for solid waste disposal continue to mount sharply. Part of the increase in cost is, naturally, a result of the growth to which I have referred. But other factors have contributed to this increase. One of these factors is the increased cost of collection resulting in large part from very necessary salary increases for traditionally low-paid sanitation workers. It is estimated that up to 80 per cent of funds spent on solid waste management goes into the collection and hauling of the waste to its final destination. Yet even with the expenditure of such a large percentage of the waste management budget on collection, we still have not advanced substantially from the days when a horse-drawn cart was the means of rubbish removal. We have simply replaced the horse with an internal combustion engine.
Another factor in the escalating cost of solid waste management has been an increase in capital cost expenditures as progressive local officials discover the need for new and improved modes of disposal of solid waste. They are finding that the old, open dump method of handling waste is not meeting the needs and higher standards of today. Yet it is disappointing to note that by far the greatest percentage of collected municipal solid waste is still disposed of in this manner.
There are a number of major disposal techniques that have been used in North America. These generally come under one of four headings: land disposal, incineration, composting and ocean disposal. Land disposal can mean anything from the worst open dumps to the most efficient sanitary landfill operation. I wish I could say that the day of the open dump was over, but as I have just indicated this is far from the case. A rat-infested, stinking heap of garbage in a gully all too often still passes for land disposal in parts of the country. On the other hand, a properly run, sanitary landfill can ultimately result in the
The Budget-Mr. Goode
creation of parkland, golf courses and other public facilities. Such landfill techniques have been extensively and successfully employed by municipalities in the greater Vancouver area.
However, problems can arise. For example, in humid climates there is a tendency for contaminated ground water immediately under the landfill to be flushed into adjacent water bodies, creating a potential pollution hazard.
An even more basic problem is encountered in trying to secure suitable landfill sites: land in and around our major urban centres is scarce and costly. Homeowners object to such facilities near built-up areas. Ecologists, quite rightly, stress the dangers involved in even the best of such schemes. Even municipalities and districts which have set aside large areas for sanitary landfill eventually realize that in doing so they have not provided a longterm solution: they have merely shifted the problem along by 10 or 20 years to the time when the landfill is completed.
The second disposal technique is incineration. This method, properly utilized, has very attractive side benefits. Among these benefits can be heat recovery to produce electric power or steam. For instance, I am informed that the newest Montreal incinerator produces steam which services most of the buildings in its immediate area. In the United States, the Combustion Power Company of Palo Alto, California, is developing a flui-dized-bed incinerator which utilizes solid waste, burned at high pressure, to produce hot gases which power a turbine driving an electric generator. It is anticipated that this incinerator will produce about 15,000 kilowatts of electric power every day while in the process of burning 400 tons of municipal waste. Experts claim that municipal solid waste constitutes a fuel with a heating value equal to approximately one-third that of good grade coal, about 5,000 British thermal units per pound. There are, however, certain drawbacks to the incineration technique. These include the polluting properties of the by-products and the fact that after most existing incineration processes, roughly 25 per cent of the waste by weight remains in the form of ashes, glass and metals.
Composting is the third disposal technique. In this process inorganic substances are separated from the organic in mixed refuse and the latter is converted to a peat-like organic fertilizer and soil conditioner. This process has proved popular in European cities such as Madrid which composts 200 tons daily, and Moscow which in recent years opened a 600-ton per day plant. The process has never been very popular in North America because the compost product tends not to be of uniform quality and because the garbage and refuse of our cities is relatively low in organic content. Finally there has been a tendency for some cities and industries to look to ocean disposal as a means of getting rid of solid waste. Fortunately, this has not been much of a problem in Canada and the provisions of the new Fisheries Act make this undesirable practice extremely unlikely in the future.
After considering these various methods it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that probably the best solution to the

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Goode
solid waste problem lies somewhere within the framework of what has been called the three R's-recovery, recycling and re-use. We have been made most vividly aware in recent years that on this planet our resources are not infinite. Just because Canada has been blessed with natural resources which are the envy of every nation on this earth does not give us the right to fritter them away. In fact, the opposite is true. We must conserve them by every means at our disposal. One of these means is the process of recycling.
When we talk of recovery, recycling and re-use it is well to bear in mind that while these processes promise much hope they are as yet far from being totally explored. At the present time most techniques for separating and recovering waste remain relatively primitive and costly. The potential results of a successful program, however, are well illustrated in an example given in a report on solid waste management prepared by Mr. J. J. Kaller for the Greater Vancouver Regional District. It reads in part as follows:
Hypothetically, a hundred thousand tons of paper per year taken out from municipal refuse collection and disposal budgets would mean close to a $1,000,000 per year saving in the cost of these services. It would also save space in the refuse dumps, create work for a salvaging company and save many acres of forests. To bring this more in perspective, it can be said that Vancouver daily papers alone can save about 10 acres of forest per day, or in the order of 3,000 acres per year. This year's Regional Districts 555,000 telephone directories, if repulped after salvaging, could save 35,000 trees.
Another dramatic example of what can be done is written up in the September, 1970, edition of "Environmental Science and Technology". According to that journal, construction should now be under way on a new $10 million solid waste reclamation plant in Newcastle county, Delaware. This plant is unique in that it will completely process 500 tons of domestic solid waste and selected industrial waste and 70 tons of sewage sludge per day and may eventually be expanded to process 1,000 tons per day. When I say completely processed, I mean that at the end of the process every bit of the solid waste will have been turned into a useful product. Ferrous metals will be removed and sold; organic wastes and sewage sludge will be turned into a high quality humus product; clean paper will be shredded, baled and sold; other paper and materials such as tires and plastics will undergo a technique which provides good quality carbon products; glass, grit, sand and non-ferrous metals will be sorted and sold. The objective is that the plant be brought as quickly as possible to the point where it is self-supporting, with the return from the reclaimed products offsetting operational costs.
Who will pay the construction costs? This, I think, is the significant point. Under a federal statute of the United States, the solid wastes resources act of 1970, pilot plants of this nature stand to receive up to 75 per cent of construction costs. What I have been trying to suggest today is that this is just the type of thing which I believe the government of Canada should be doing. I have outlined a number of problem areas in which the government could usefully employ funds for research, training, demonstration of new technology, technical assistance and grants for local, regional and provincial solid waste planning programs. Our neighbour to the south is doing this very thing, even though until the passage of the solid waste disposal act of 1965 local governments there, as here, have traditionally carried the primary responsibility for solid waste collection, processing and disposal with no assistance from the senior government. In other words, they are far ahead of us.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, a program such as I would like to see implemented would undoubtedly cost money but it would be money very well spent. I end with the following remark by the Conservation Council of Ontario which makes the point especially well:
We are living in a highly complex world and the answers we will find will entail difficult choices, and they will cost money. Conservation is a matter of intelligent choices which will benefit mankind's own long-term interests and be in harmony with his environment. But we must choose, and we cannot afford not to pay the cost. Economic yardsticks can no longer be the major criterion in our decisions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we often say when we rise on an occasion like this that we had no intention of speaking, but the previous speaker, to whom I listened very attentively, referred in particular to pollution. I have good news, I think probably the only good news that this House has had on this subject for many months. Today in Lethbridge the weather is particularly nice; it is in the high 50s. The snow is melting and nothing but good, clean snow water is draining gently into the river systems. I hope this will make my friend on the opposite side feel better.
I want to speak on several subjects, the main one being unemployment, a subject which most of us have tackled, as well as the OAS, the just society, Indians and agriculture. I say right at the outset that I have great respect for the office of the Prime Minister of Canada. Some time ago I felt very proud when one morning I heard a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I have always been proud of the office of the Prime Minister. There are some things that have taken place right here in this House, however, that lead me to be somewhat critical of the present occupant of that office.
I mentioned earlier that I wished to say something about unemployment. This reminds me of a cartoon that I saw in a newspaper two or three weeks ago which showed the Prime Minister as a goal tender with the net behind him almost completely filled with pucks labelled "Unemployed". The referee depicted in the cartoon was the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), a greatly respected man, in a striped shirt. The caption read: "Are you interested in the score?" I think the cartoon well describes the debate today. Certainly the leader of the government must be interested in the score. But why are all these items piling up day after day, week after week and year after year?
I wanted to say something about agriculture and I think now is a good time to do so because early today, during the question period, the Prime Minister said, in answer to a question from a member of the opposition

February 10, 1971

relating to agriculture, that if the opposition were not so slow, the government would have moved more quickly. I regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is not in the chamber at the moment. I recall that on many occasions he has told us that all ten provinces agreed to the bill that he was sponsoring. He even asked a committee of the House to travel throughout the country in two different years. It was a very expensive procedure. But even with all that, the public did not go along with his marketing bill. The government did not bow to the slowness of the opposition; it bowed to public opinion.
I recall an experience with a former Minister of Agriculture, a westerner whom I respected. He fought for western Canada. I do not mean that a minister of agriculture necessarily should fight for one particular region or area. On that occasion the then Prime Minister said the opposition was being very slow, and the reply given to him was: "The Minister of Agriculture has less regard for the facts than a tom-cat has for a marriage licence." People in agriculture feel the same way.
The Prime Minister has placed the blame for many things on the opposition. He does not seem to have particular regard for the facts. At one time reference was made to members of the House of Commons to the effect that they were a bunch of bums. I have been a member of this House for a long time, Mr. Speaker: the people who represent the Canadian public are not bums. I know some hon. members of the House have been bumming around the world lately. They have been promoting Canada as a peacemaker throughout the world yet under the present administration we cannot look after our own affairs. They have been bumming around the world giving away money interest free. I shall have something to say about the interest that Canadians pay on money they borrow.
Returning to the question of unemployment, I would point out that we have the highest rate of unemployment in the western world. We have the highest rate of unemployment, percentagewise, related to population that Canada has ever known. It has been said that the thirties were our worst era in that respect, but I repeat that today we have the highest rate of unemployment percentagewise that our country has ever known. For years we have been told that the opposition has been at fault. I have heard many good suggestions made by members of the opposition, but they have not been accepted. I am scared at what is happening. Where are we going? Our country is becoming more divided. We are getting more unemployment. Interest rates are rising higher and higher, and all we hear is excuses.
I was happy to hear the announcement made by the minister responsible for housing. I am convinced this is one key to the solution of our unemployment situation. I would like to mention one case relating to unemployment, housing and OAS. I have here a communication that I received from a senior citizen in Ottawa. There are thousands like her across the country. She is a lady who is 82 years old, the widow of a former captain in the Ottawa fire department who retired after 42 years service, and
The Budget-Mr. Gundlock
whose pension lapsed when he died. Today she receives $133.61 a month, everything combined. Her rent is $117.50, leaving her $16.11 per month for food and clothing. This is the situation in the capital city, but there are thousands of people like this all across the country. She has been notified that on March 1 her rent will be raised by $10 a month, leaving her $6.11. I think $117.50 is a pretty high rent for a 100-year old building in centre town.
I was happy to hear what the minister said today but I have heard it many times. Had the scheme started even two or three years ago this senior citizen could be living quite nicely at half the rent. That kind of rent should allow for a nice new apartment, perhaps with a sauna bath and swimming pool. This situation is not confined to Ottawa but applies to my own city of Lethbridge. Why do we have so many announcements? Why do they tie up this tremendous building fund for years and years? The government says that we never offer anything, we are just a bunch of bums. Referring to the cartoon which appeared recently in the Hamilton Spectator, showing the Prime Minister with a net full of pucks, I ask why the devil he is piling up all this stuff. The thought which occurs to me rather scares me. If money were free for housing, a lot more people would be employed directly and indirectly: many thousands would be employed, including young people. But all we hear is talk.
I want to have a word about unemployment, particularly of young people. I mentioned the thirties. That was the last time we had unemployment that could be compared with today. No one can challenge my figures when I say that unemployment is higher today than it was in the thirties, percentagewise. We all know that the biggest force of unemployed is the medium-aged who have families to support. I have been through that myself. There has been a lot of talk about the young unemployed, and we all wonder what they are thinking. I believe they feel that the government of Canada has allowed foreign capital and foreign ownership to dominate the resources of this country to the point where we are controlled from outside. When we say foreign control we immediately think of the United States, but when we speak of winning battles against that country all we have to do is walk down the corridor opposite the library where a brass plaque commemorates the war between Canada and the United States. In that war we won over 20 battles; in fact, we won the war. We can do it again, but not the way this government is going.
We want to develop this country and keep it Canadian, but when you get on a train, bus or airplane you meet people from the United States who are interested in developing and investing in Canada. This is simply because this government-and I lay this at the feet of the Prime Minister-allows tax concessions to foreign countries investing in Canada that are not allowed to Canadians. These young people ask a legitimate question, Mr. Speaker, and I think they should have an answer. If Canadians were given even a part of the concessions allowed foreign investors, Canadians would control their own resources as never before.

February 10, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Gundlock
I wish to say something about the just society that we have heard so much about. With all this unemployment I am beginning to wonder if there is even a society. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) here and I want to say that I have a great deal of respect for him. However, unemployment will get worse before it gets better. I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker-and I hoped someone would challenge my remarks-that we are experiencing the worst unemployment in Canadian history. One wonders just how to define the just society. If unemployment becomes much worse, one may have to say, "We have just had a society." That is what scares me. We have drifted. Surely the government, which rests squarely on the shoulders of the Prime Minister, cannot blame other people for being too slow in this area. I do not want to go over the details-we have all heard them before-but if we go on like this much more I am afraid that what I nave suggested may happen.
In conclusion may I say a word about a matter that ties in with unemployment. The other day we were told about the treatment of locals employed in the Northwest Territories. I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development ever since coming to Ottawa. I know that the allegation is true. I have sat in many committees and we were often promised that discrimination would no longer take place. I should not put it that strongly, perhaps. We were assured that it would no longer take place; there would be a conference among all departments in order to see that local, and particularly native people, would be fully employed.
The report the other day showed that people from southern Canada had been employed up there at between $12 and $15 a day in dragging chains. They were employed in surveying. To the native people, and particularly to Eskimos, such a sum would be a pretty nice stake: it would improve their lot. They are not educated in the sense used when we refer to educated people. They have no degrees; they have no secondary education. Nevertheless they are educated in the sense that they know how to survive and how to adapt to conditions, and that sort of thing. Why should they not be given that sort of job? I sat on the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates when it was considering on November 26, 1970, the supplementary estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I tried then to introduce a question that had to do with the welfare of Indians and Eskimos.
I spoke of the death of an infant on the Blood reserve, Alberta, last September. The death was looked into by the chief coroner of Alberta, which shows how serious this matter was. In the coroner's inquest it was said that when the parents brought the young child to the hospital, they found a locked door. I am referring to the Indian hospital on the Blood reserve in Alberta. This was drawn to the attention of the minister when the committee was considering supplementary estimates. In addition it was learned that the parents were at one point refused the use of a telephone. They simply wanted to call a doctor.

It was also drawn to the chief coroner's attention that
the attending physician had said much later that if he could have attended earlier, the death might not have happened. I referred all the details to the minister. The minister said that he could not accept any responsibility, that it was the responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Nevertheless, after insistence on the part of some members he agreed to call the matter to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This was an accident, he said. I do not think it was an accident, Mr. Speaker. A few days later, when the supplementary estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare were being considered, I asked whether the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development had transferred this matter to the Department of National Health and Welfare and was told that the latter department had not heard of it.
We have been discussing this and that matter and talking about reorganization of the government. To me, this will only give more jobs to people opposite. At a time when there is unemployment and suffering we are talking about reorganization and the additional expenditure that will be involved. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if the members of this government are really communicating one with the other. I have given one example of what I mean but there are many others. We are asked to reorganize the government, but there is no communication between departments. We talk about reorganizing the government, but what is the use of establishing new departments if there is lack of communication between them? I think this situation will get worse. I have tried to bring forward my points and alternatives that could be taken. There is nothing new in them. With those words, Mr. Speaker, I shall sit down.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes remaining today I want to use the latitude that is extended to us in this debate to direct my remarks entirely to one subject, agriculture. A concern for agriculture, its problems and people is not, of course, as Your Honour knows, limited to Canada: it appears to be increasing throughout the world. The roots of the concern are indicated by the words hunger, malnutrition, surplus, poverty, disparity, credit, markets, power, integration and information. With respect to those words Canada is no exception; the root words are found here too.
Many studies have been made in the past two or three years to identify agriculture's problems, analyse alternatives and recommend changes which, hopefully, will permit the realization of existing and future opportunities for food, feed and fibre and will increase the farmer's share of Canada's wealth. I want to take the liberty that is extended to me by participating in the debate to put on record a few statistics. By virtue of this being the House of Commons, I hope that these comments will receive a hearing in segments of the Canadian social structure other than agriculture. I am convinced that there is a vast breakdown in communication and understanding between agriculture and industry, especially the prime producers and the so-called urban people and consumers in general.
February 10, 1971

The most recent statistics indicate that in Canada there are in excess of 430,000 farm holdings, of which approximately 100,000 are commercial farms. There are 95,000 farms with sales of more than $10,000 per year, and 119,500 farms which paid federal income tax. Wheat and livestock farms account for one half of the commercial farm census, and dairy farms account for one-fifth. The total farmland area is 174 million acres. Eighty per cent of the total agricultural land is in western Canada. The total investment in Canadian agriculture of farm operators was estimated to be $22.4 billion in 1968, the most recent year for which statistics are available, or approximately $41,000 per worker, excluding rented land and buildings. New capital formation in agriculture is estimated to be approximately $1 billion a year, or approximately eight per cent of the new capital formation. The sources of new capital available to agriculture are varied, but a few sources predominate.
The farm labour force numbered 1,096,000 persons in 1948, 22 per cent of the total employed Canadian labour force. In 1968, 20 years later, this number had dropped to 546,000, or seven per cent of a much larger labour force. Capital inputs, compared to labour and real estate inputs, have increased from about one third of the total input in the period 1948-52 to over 50 per cent in recent years. The primary agricultural industry has become one which is highly dependent upon the non-farm or off-farm sector for supplies and services. Agribusiness is a term used to describe the non-farm industries which produce goods and services for farm use and those industries engaged in the process of raw materials of farm origin. Employment in the agribusiness industry, which includes food processing, tobacco manufacturing, leather goods, manufacture of implements and fertilizers, etc., has been estimated at
338,000	persons, or about 60 per cent of the employment in the farm or primary producer sector.
The two groups, the on-farm or primary producer and the off-farm producers, comprise about 12 per cent of the Canadian labour force. It is important for Canadians who are not familiar with or have not been interested in agriculture to recognize that approximately 18 per cent of the total rail freight in our country is comprised of farm products. Agricultural commodities represent exact-
The Budget-Mr. McBride
ly one quarter of the tonnage moved through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Farm expenditures on fuel and lubricants are equal to approximately 17 per cent of the total sales of motor fuels for use in motor vehicles. In the wholesale trade field, almost one quarter of the persons employed owe their employment to the sale of farm products, food products or farm supplies.
The most recent statistics indicate that $2.5 billion value added by the food and beverage industries represents 57 per cent of the cash receipts from farming, or $4.3 billion. In other words, Canadian farmers receive $4.3 billion. The food is taken off the farm and certain processes or actions are carried out. By the time it reaches the consumer, it increases in value by $2.5 billion, or 57 per cent of the original price. The food and beverage industry, compared with the paper, chemical, electrical, transportation and metal fabricating industries, employs the most people, pays the largest amount of wages and salaries, spends more on materials and supplies, ships goods of its own manufacture exceeding $7 billion and has by far the largest total value added, $2.5 billion in 1966.
Changes in agriculture during economic growth are influenced directly by the developments in food marketing. The most significant of these for agriculture is the rapid growth of large market-oriented food processors and distributors. The market-oriented firm, in contrast to traditional production-oriented business such as farming tries to discover what consumers want and to design an integrated research-product-package-promotion-distribution operation to meet these demands. In its outlook on operations it gives priority to consumers and marketing over production and procurement. This is especially true and relevant when the basic product that needs to be procured is produced in surplus and is easily available. As a result, farmers are increasingly called upon to tailor farm production to meet the dynamic, more exciting requirements of modern markets.

February 10, 1971
Constitutional Conference Third Working Session Ottawa, February 8 and 9, 1971 Statement of Conclusions

General
1.	In accordance with the conclusion of their working session last September, the First Ministers gave priority to the questions of an amending formula and an early patriation of the Canadian Constitution. The Conference agreed that the Government of Canada and the provinces should proceed as quickly as possible to patriate the Constitution, with an appropriate amending formula applicable entirely within Canada, and with such other changes as can be agreed upon quickly. This approach would permit a substantial degree of progress to be made quickly, while work on other aspects of constitutional revision continues. The First Ministers considered that such action might incorporate the elements set forth in the following paragraphs. However, the First Ministers reserved their right to further analyze all the juridical and other implications.
Patriation of the Constitution
2.	The Constitutional Conference agreed on a procedure to be undertaken in Canada at a very early date in order to bring home the Constitution and to transfer to the people of Canada, through their elected representatives the exclusive power to amend and to enact constitutional provisions affecting Canada. This procedure would involve:
(a)	Agreement among the governments as to changes and procedure.
(b)	Approval of a resolution in the usual way, by legislatures plus the two Houses of Parliament, authorizing the issuance of a proclamation by the Governor General to contain the amendment formula and whatever changes are agreed upon.
(c)	Recommendation that the British Parliament legislate to:
(i)	recognize the legal validity of the Canadian proclamation and its provisions;
(ii)	provide that no future British law should have application to Canada; and
(iii)	make any consequential repeal or amendment of British statutes affecting the Canadian Constitution.
(d)	Issuance of the proclamation by the Governor General on a date to coincide with the effective date of the British law.
The Amending Formula
3.	The Constitutional Conference has considered the nature of the formula which should be adopted to permit
the Canadian Constitution to be amended wholly within Canada. The First Ministers agreed that the following formula was a feasible approach.
I.	General Procedure
All constitutional amendments in future, except those covered in II and III, would require a resolution of consent at the federal level plus consent of the legislatures of a majority of the provinces of Canada including.
(a)	the legislature of any province now containing at least 25 per cent of the population of Canada, and of any other province that hereafter contains 25 per cent of the population of Canada; and
(b)	the legislatures of at least two provinces west of Ontario providing that the consenting provinces comprise 50 per cent of the population of the provinces west of Ontario and the legislatures of at least two provinces east of Quebec.
II.	Federal and Provincial Constitutions
Sections 91(1) and 92(1) would be repealed and replaced by a section giving the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the provinces power to amend their respective Constitutions except with regard to the following matters when the general procedure set out in I would apply:
(a)	the functions of the Queen, Governor General and Lieutenant Governors;
(b)	need for annual sessions;
(c)	maximum period between elections; (The above three would apply to the legislatures as well as to Parliament; the following would apply to Parliament only.)
(d)	principle of proportionate and minimum representation of members of Parliament from the provinces in the House of Commons.
(e)	the number and residence qualification of Senators representing each province, and the powers of the Senate.
III.	Amendments of Concern to Canada plus One or More but not All Provinces
Such changes would require a resolution of consent at the federal level plus the consent of the legislatures of the provinces concerned.
Fundamental Rights
4.	It was agreed to entrench in the Constitution the following basic political rights:
February 10, 1971

(a)	universal suffrage and free, democratic elections at least every five years;
(b)	freedom of thought, conscience and religion;
(c)	freedom of opinion and expression; and
(d)	freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
The exercise of these freedoms may be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law and as are reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety, health or morals or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others.
Language Rights
5.	It was agreed that English and French should be declared the official languages of Canada, with the following provisions that would have equal application in all parts of Canada and to both languages:
(a)	Any person may use English or French:
(i)	in the Debates of Parliament and, with reservations expressed by some provinces, in the
legislatures;
(ii)	in any pleading or process in federal courts;
(iii)	in communication with the federal administration.
(b)	Federal statutes and instruments shall be in both languages.
(c)	The individual shall have the right to have English or French as his main language of instruction in publicly supported schools in areas where the language of instruction of his choice is chosen by a sufficient number of persons to justify the provision of the necessary facilities. It was recognized that some further consideration will have to be given by various governments in order to determine appropriate administrative arrangements to implement the provision, what constitutes a "sufficient number", and what should be the percentage of instruction in the main language. Quebec lodged a general reservation with respect to this sub-paragraph pending an examination of all its implications.
(d)	Parliament or a legislature may accord further recognition to the two languages.
Supreme Court
6.	It was agreed that the existence and the independence of the Supreme Court of Canada should be entrenched in the Constitution, which should also provide for its basic structure. Its jurisdiction would continue to be that of a court of final appeal for the country. It was also agreed that, while the Federal Government should retain the power of appointment to the court, the Constitution should recognize the importance of provincial participation in the process of selection of suitable candidates for appointment. It was also concluded that study should be given to the means of assuring the availability on the court of civil law judges to hear civil law appeals. It was agreed, in addition, that there should be discussion of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear appeals in matters of strictly provincial law.
Regional Disparities
7.	Recalling their conclusion on the subject of regional disparities at the working session in September, the First Ministers agreed that the Constitution should include a recognition of the importance of equality of opportunity for all Canadians. It was therefore concluded that the reduction of regional disparities should be referred to both in a new preamble and in the body of the Constitution.
(a)	The preamble should state that one objective of Confederation is the social, economic, and cultural development, and the general welfare and equality of opportunity for all citizens in whatever region they may live;
(b)	In the body of the Constitution there should be a statement of obligation on all governments, federal and provincial
(i)	to promote equality of opportunity and wellbeing for all individuals;
(ii)	to ensure, as nearly as possible, that essential public services of reasonable quality will be available to individual citizens.
(iii)	to promote economic development which will reduce disparities in the social and economic opportunities of individual Canadians in whatever region they may live.
This obligation would not be enforceable by the Courts and would not have the effect of altering the distribution of legislative powers.
Mechanisms of Federal-Provincial Relations
8.	It was agreed that the revised Constitution should contain a provision, probably in the preamble, recognizing the important role of intergovernmental consultation and cooperation in the effective working of Canadian federalism. Also, in order to provide for the basic mechanisms of federal-provincial consultation, there should be a specific provision that the Government of Canada shall at least once a year consult with provincial governments about the desirability of holding a Conference of First Ministers.
Modernization of the Constitution
9.	Finally, the First Ministers agreed that work will be undertaken between now and the next meeting of the Constitutional Conference in June to propose specific alterations in the Constitution such as a new preamble and the deletion of spent and irrelevant provisions. Specific proposals in this respect will be brought forward for consideration by the Conference in June.
Next Step
10.	It was recognized that the next steps would include further bilateral discussions leading up to the next meeting of First Ministers, and in addition as required, the on-going coordinating work of the Continuing Committee of Officials.

February 10, 1971

Social Policy
1.	The Conference heard the views of the Government of Quebec on social policy in general and income security in particular. Quebec emphasized a broad conception of social policy and the importance of fitting income security measures into a global integrated policy with the objective of meeting effectively the problem of poverty. The Conference expressed its sympathy for this basic social objective. Quebec emphasized the fact that the existing distribution of legislative powers cannot be maintained if it impedes the realization of that objective. In addition, Quebec considers that the question of social policy is a fundamental element of the constitutional revision as a whole.
2.	The federal government for its part expressed its desire to coordinate its income security measures with the social policies of the provinces in order that each provincial government as well as the federal government may best realize its social objectives. There is and should continue to be room for different social policies in different provinces.
3.	In regard to the Quebec proposals in particular, the federal government noted that what was suggested in regard to family allowances was very similar to the proposed federal Family Income Security Plan. The Quebec statement also indicated that the Old Age Security Pension and Guaranteed Income Supplement would fit into its plans. Similar improvements in the Quebec and Canada Pension Plans have also been proposed.
4.	Already decisions have been made to modify certain features of the proposals for amending the Unemployment Insurance Act on the basis of the information and arguments advanced by Quebec Ministers. Only in the case of the General Social Allowance Plan does there appear to be the necessity for further time and study to ascertain what is practicable during the near future.
5.	The Conference was informed that bilateral discussions had already been planned between provincial and federal ministers and officials on these matters and their possible constitutional implications, and a further meeting of the Ministers of Welfare on income security was scheduled several months from now. The First Ministers asked that this work be accelerated and that the Ministers of Welfare report to the meeting of the First Ministers in June.
Canadian Interprovincial Marketing
6.	Reference was made to current problems being encountered in connection with interprovincial marketing of certain agricultural products. The view was expressed that the problem had still not been solved, since the last discussion in September, and some provinces suggested that the Federal Government should exercise existing
constitutional powers to deal with the matter. A further suggestion by some provinces was that provincial marketing boards should retract certain regulations that affect the freedom of movement of goods, but another view was that this could not be done unless other action were taken to replace such regulations and avoid harm to local agricultural industries. In this connection, it was suggested that the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill, now before Parliament could facilitate a satisfactory resolution of the problem.
7.	It was also observed that the question of interprovincial trade was a fundamental constitutional question which should be examined at a later meeting of the Conference.
Environmental Management-Pollution
8.	The Constitutional Conference examined proposals for constitutional changes in jurisdiction related to the control of pollution.
9.	In particular, the First Ministers considered a federal proposal that there should be a new concurrent power for Parliament and the provincial legislatures to make laws in relation to the control of pollution of air and water. Under this proposal, if there were a conflict between a federal law made under this power and a provincial law made under it, the federal law would prevail when it applies to control pollution which has, or if permitted would have, significant international or interprovincial effects, but in other circumstances the provincial law would prevail over the federal law.
10.	Some First Ministers expressed interest in this proposal. Another view, however, was that new provisions could better be considered after there has been more experience in dealing with pollution; in the meantime, it would be preferable to rely on improved arrangements for coordination and cooperation between governments based upon existing constitutional provisions. A further view was that areas of exclusive federal and provincial jurisdiction would be preferable to the general concurrency which has been proposed.
11.	It was agreed that the implications of various constitutional approaches should be given further study.
Other Business
12.	The Conference received a report from the Continuing Committee of Officials on Paramountcy as Applied to Public Retirement Insurance, and accepted the recommendations regarding additional study.
Next Meeting
13.	The Constitutional Conference confirmed that it would meet next on June 14-16 in Victoria and that the meeting would be public, at least in part.
February 10, 1971

NON-CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS Unemployment
1. The First Ministers discussed the unemployment situation across Canada, and expressed their concern for the problems being encountered by many Canadians this winter. Several First Ministers urged the Government of Canada to take additional action to alleviate the problem.
2.	The Minister of Finance of Canada outlined the policies of the Government of Canada to combat unemployment, and stated that present indicators point to increasing economic growth and declining unemployment as the year progresses. He stressed that over-reaction would aggravate the problem by causing a resurgence of the inflationary spiral.
3.	It was generally agreed that the federal and provincial governments should consult together concerning any possible additional steps which might be taken to alleviate the present situation.
